name: The Gilbert household — an inferred labourer (north division)
head: inf_labourer_north_08

arrival.note: NOT AN ARRIVAL, A BOUND. Nothing dates a hypothesised household, and a year would be a claim nobody made. `not_later_than` the scene date states the only thing the inference carries: the town's need is measured on 1 July 1835, so the household is posited as being here by then and at no stated time before it.

party_size_on_arrival.note: Not claimed. The layer infers households, not families: the person entries here are the ones the trade argument requires and nothing counts wives or children, because counting them would multiply a hypothesis by an invention.

origin.note: Not claimed. Where a hypothesised resident came from is unknowable by construction, and the documented layer's origins (Vermont, Washington, Ann Arbor) are evidence about those men and not a distribution to sample from.

reason_for_coming.note: Not claimed for the person. The reason the HOUSEHOLD is in the dataset is the trade argument in research_note, which is a statement about the town and not about a motive.

lives_at.note: THE HOUSEHOLD IS HOUSED, WHICH IS THE POINT OF THE LAYER. recon_1835_north_d1_060 is an anonymous inferred roof already standing on the plat, adopted rather than duplicated: its existence, position and footprint stay conjectural and the adoption adds only the occupant argument. Which roof of the right family and district a hypothesised household occupies is not evidence about that roof; the household needed a dwelling and the programme assigned it one.

works_at.note: NO SEPARATE WORKPLACE. A labourer in this town worked in other people's buildings, in the street, or in the dwelling itself, and inventing a shop for the sake of a link would be inventing a building.

present_on_scene_date.note: Presence on the scene date IS the hypothesis: this household exists in the dataset because the town of 1 July 1835 demonstrably needed households of this trade. It is not a finding about anybody's whereabouts.

persons.name: Nathaniel Gilbert

occupation.note: THE LARGEST TRADE IN ANY WESTERN TOWN AND THE ONE NO ROSTER RECORDS, because a labourer advertises nothing, holds no office and joins no church committee - the three ways almost every documented person in this dataset became documented. The harbour works were under construction through 1834 and 1835 (both piers are structure records here), the streets were being graded, and several hundred buildings were being raised. Twelve labouring households are inferred - the largest single group in this layer and still a small fraction of what 3,265 people implies - and every one of them is housed in the meanest roof the schedule carries: a D1 log cabin or a D2 plank shanty.

name_basis.value: invented from the New England and New York pool
name_basis.note: THE NAME IS INVENTED. No source names this resident, and this field is not a finding about anybody — it is a label so that a reconstructed household reads as a household rather than as a row in a table. It was drawn from the New England and New York pool in data/reconstruction/1835_invented_name_pools.json, which is seeded from the names of the 76 ATTESTED residents this project holds — real people, named from cited sources — so that an invented resident is named the way this town's documented residents were actually named rather than the way a story would name one. The community was drawn WITHOUT a weighting that any source supports. An even draw on purpose. The Irish labouring population that later defines this trade in Chicago arrives with the canal contracts of 1836, AFTER the scene date, so weighting 1835 labourers Irish would be importing a later decade into this one. The evidence for the pool itself: The dominant documented group in this dataset by a wide margin. Attested origins among the named residents include Vermont (three households), Washington County Vermont, Burlington, Connecticut by way of Detroit, Sackett's Harbor New York, Guilford Vermont, and 'New England'. Attested surnames of this stock in the town include Harmon, Taylor, Brown, Davis, Porter, Wright, Blodgett, Carpenter, Carver, Caton, Calhoun, Peck, Dole, Newberry and Bates.

research_note: INFERRED HOUSEHOLD - eighth of 12 labourer households in this layer, in the north division. THE LARGEST TRADE IN ANY WESTERN TOWN AND THE ONE NO ROSTER RECORDS, because a labourer advertises nothing, holds no office and joins no church committee - the three ways almost every documented person in this dataset became documented. The harbour works were under construction through 1834 and 1835 (both piers are structure records here), the streets were being graded, and several hundred buildings were being raised. Twelve labouring households are inferred - the largest single group in this layer and still a small fraction of what 3,265 people implies - and every one of them is housed in the meanest roof the schedule carries: a D1 log cabin or a D2 plank shanty. METHOD: the count comes from the occupation census in data/reconstruction/1835_inferred_household_programme.json, which calibrates every trade against three things this project already holds - the 1835 town census (3,265 people, 398 dwellings), Andreas's roster of the fall of 1833 (about fifty named people, most with a trade, in a settlement of some 350), and the reconstruction specification's roof schedule, whose workshop and store family targets are treated as the ceiling on a trade rather than as its measure. Every count is stated NET of the documented layer: this dataset infers a tradesman only where it cannot name one.
